tier_reason: The README's Benchmarks section (added by the author kolemannix in 'Add benchmark results (#4)', 2026-03-04) shows raw output of the public lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark harness (benchmarks/benchmark.cpp and benchmarks/benchmark32.cpp, which call strtod_l/strtof_l with a C locale) with strtod/strtof columns, so the code is public, but the CPU is only 'Apple silicon' and no compiler versions are given, so it falls short of A; first-party run, so C.

corrections.baseline: strtod_l / strtof_l with a C locale from the platform libc (the harness calls these, not plain strtod); on the Apple silicon test machine that is the macOS libc, which the README does not name
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang for all runs except benchmark32, which the README says ran with gcc (on macOS the gcc command normally invokes Apple clang); no compiler versions stated. The harness (lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark) CMakeLists defaults to the Release build type (CMake's -O3 -DNDEBUG for Clang/GCC) and builds the benchmark targets as C++17 with ffc.h included under FFC_IMPL in the C++ translation unit; no -march flags. The ffc.h repo Makefile builds tests with clang -O3 -std=c99, which is not the benchmark build.
corrections.hardware: Apple silicon Mac; the harness prints 'loaded db: as3 (Apple silicon)' (the name of the performance-counter database, not a chip model) and clock readings of about 3.7-4.1 GHz; exact chip model not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 209 stars, 12 forks; valkey uses it in src/valkey_strtod.h (confirmed at the README's pinned commit and on valkey's unstable branch); the README also cites hiredis pull request #1328 (not opened)
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from one Apple silicon machine with no compiler versions and no chip model; the baseline is the macOS libc strtod_l with a C locale, so the roughly 1.6-2x speedup says nothing direct about glibc or musl strtod, and no x86 or Linux numbers against strtod are published. Most of the win belongs to the fast_float algorithm: ffc is a C99 port and is only 1.06-1.15x faster than C++ fast_float in the same README table (derived from page data). The README numbers are dated 2026-03-03 and predate correctness fixes (#26, a value-kind mismatch in the float slow path, 2026-06-15; a Clang -0.0 result under FE_DOWNWARD fixed in #24) and several performance PRs (#23, #24, #25, #32), so they do not describe the current header and are probably understated. PR #24 (2026-06-30, fcostaoliveira) reports GCC -O3 numbers on AWS Graviton4 and Xeon Platinum 8488C from an unpublished ffc-only microbenchmark, against earlier ffc and fast_float only (for example mesh.txt 1656 MB/s on Graviton4, '+231%' versus fastfloat; random [0,1] tied with fastfloat on the Xeon), with no strtod column. The harness only checks that each parse succeeds, not that values match the other parsers (ffc has its own exhaustive binary32 and supplemental tests). Port of fast_float, which is already catalogued; the orchestrator may treat it as a duplicate under the port rule, although it is a separate C99 implementation with production adoption in valkey.

notes: All README numbers match the record exactly (ratios 1.95x, 1.59x, 1.68x, 1.97x vs strtod/strtof and 1.13x vs fastfloat are correctly derived); license (Apache-2.0 OR MIT OR BSL-1.0), stars 209, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-02 confirmed. The ffc rows come from Daniel Lemire's own harness, which added ffc on 2026-03-03 (upstream HEAD includes it for non-MSVC compilers; the kolemannix fork limits it to __clang__), but the run itself was published by the ffc author, so tier stays C. Shortcomings to record: macOS-libc-only baseline, no chip model or compiler versions, stale numbers that predate correctness fixes and later optimizations, small margin over fast_float (1.06-1.15x), and a likely duplicate as a port of fast_float.
